question: Safeguarding a heritage tree species (Pinus Pinea L.) and public health in the Metropolitan City of Rome

Over the last two years, initiatives to cut down 20 000 trees and replant 10 % of that number in and around Rome have used up significant public resources. Many of the pine groves that had long been a feature of Rome’s historic centre and parks have also gone, as have a number of large pine forests in Ostia. Again, nothing has been done to restore these areas. In the light of the above, could the Commission answer the following questions: 1.

Given that Ostia’s coastline has lost thousands of hectares’ worth of pine forests to a combination of fires and parasite infestations, can local authorities use resources under the EU Solidarity Fund to remedy the situation?

Will the Commission implement any plans for the reforestation of urban areas and the safeguarding of heritage species likePinus Pinea L.,and could rules be adopted to restrict the unjustified felling ofPinus Pinea L.trees and promote restoration efforts?

What impact does the Commission think the mass clearing of trees is having on public health, and would it make a connection between this and the recent alarming findings that show the air in Milan, Rome and the Po Valley to be unbreathable?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.6.2024) 1. The EU Solidarity Fund (EUSF)1 can be activated at the request of a Member State in case of a major natural disaster such as earthquakes, floods, droughts, forest fires, within specific deadlines and thresholds of estimated damages specified in Article 2 Regulation (EC) No 2012/2002. Man-made disasters are not eligible for EUSF support. 2.

The European Regional Development Fund programme for Lazio 2021-20272 does not foresee or exclude a specific action for reforestation with pine trees. Selection of operations under shared management is the responsibility of the national institutions implementing the programme3. The Commission also launched a pledge to plant 3 billion additional trees by 2030 and encouraged Member States’ authorities to contribute.

3. Forest and trees in urban areas are important for biodiversity and key allies in the fight against climate change through their capacity to remove and store carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. Increasing carbon sinks across the EU is an important component of the transition to climate neutrality by 2050.
Under the revised Land Use, Land Use Change and Forestry regulation4, Member States have committed to national targets to increase carbon removals through inter alia forests by 2030.

The Carbon Removal Certification Framework will support land managers5 to undertake measures such as sustainable reforestation and improved forest management practices by mobilising additional private funding from the voluntary carbon market. The Ambient Air Quality Directives6 set standards for a number of air pollutants.
The choice of measures to achieve those standards, including in relation to forest management, is up to the Member States to decide.
